title: Thermochemistry & Spontaneity (Second Law, Entropy, & Gibbs Free Energy)
syllabus: Second law of thermodynamics; Spontaneous and non-spontaneous processes; Entropy (S) as a state function and measure of randomness; Entropy changes for reversible and irreversible processes, phase transitions, and ideal gas expansions (ΔS = n C_v ln(T2/T1) + n R ln(V2/V1)); Total entropy change (ΔS_total = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings) and criteria for spontaneity; Gibbs free energy (G = H - TS) and Gibbs-Helmholtz equation; Criteria for spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure (ΔG < 0); Effect of temperature on reaction spontaneity; Standard Gibbs energy change (ΔG°) and its relationship to equilibrium constant (K_eq); Third law of thermodynamics and absolute entropies

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] For a chemical reaction, $\Delta H = -40.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S = -80.0\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$. The temperature above which the reaction becomes non-spontaneous is:
questions.solution:
The criterion for spontaneity at constant $T$ and $P$ is $\Delta G < 0$:
$$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S < 0$$
For an exothermic reaction ($\Delta H < 0$) with decrease in entropy ($\Delta S < 0$), the reaction is spontaneous at low temperatures and becomes non-spontaneous when $\Delta G > 0$.
At equilibrium ($	ransitional temperature$):
$$\Delta G = 0 \implies T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$$
Substitute the values:
$$T = \frac{-40.0 \times 10^3\text{ J/mol}}{-80.0\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}} = 500\text{ K}$$
For $T > 500\text{ K}$, $T\Delta S$ becomes more negative, causing $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S > 0$.
Thus, the reaction is non-spontaneous above $500\text{ K}$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] For the process $\text{H}_2\text{O}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ at $1\text{ atm}$ and $260\text{ K}$, the correct signs of $\Delta H$, $\Delta S$, and $\Delta G$ are respectively:
questions.solution:
1. Melting of ice is an endothermic process (requires heat), so $\Delta H > 0$.
2. The transition from a structured solid crystal to a disordered liquid increases randomness, so $\Delta S > 0$.
3. The normal melting point of ice at $1\text{ atm}$ is $273.15\text{ K}$ ($0^\circ\text{C}$).
At $260\text{ K}$ (which is below the freezing point), the spontaneous process is the freezing of liquid water to solid ice. Hence, the melting process is non-spontaneous, meaning $\Delta G > 0$.
Therefore, $\Delta H > 0$, $\Delta S > 0$, and $\Delta G > 0$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] The entropy change ($\Delta S$) for the isothermal reversible expansion of $1\text{ mole}$ of an ideal gas from a pressure of $10\text{ atm}$ to $1\text{ atm}$ at $300\text{ K}$ is: (Take $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, $\ln 10 = 2.303$)
questions.solution:
For an ideal gas undergoing an isothermal process ($T_1 = T_2$):
$$\Delta S = n C_p \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) - n R \ln\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)$$
Since $T_1 = T_2$, the first term is zero:
$$\Delta S = -n R \ln\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right) = n R \ln\left(\frac{P_1}{P_2}\right)$$
Substitute $n = 1\text{ mol}$, $P_1 = 10\text{ atm}$, and $P_2 = 1\text{ atm}$:
$$\Delta S = 1 \times 8.314 \times \ln(10) = 8.314 \times 2.303 = +19.147\text{ J/K} \approx +19.14\text{ J/K}$$
(Expansion increases the volume and available microstates, so entropy increases).

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] For a reaction at $300\text{ K}$, the equilibrium constant is $K = 10^2$. The standard Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G^\circ$ is: (Take $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, $\ln 10 = 2.303$)
questions.solution:
The relationship between standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant is:
$$\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K = -2.303 RT \log_{10} K$$
Substitute $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, $T = 300\text{ K}$, and $K = 10^2$:
$$\Delta G^\circ = -2.303 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times \log_{10}(10^2)$$
$$\Delta G^\circ = -2.303 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times 2 = -11488.5\text{ J/mol} \approx -11.49\text{ kJ/mol}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] In which of the following reactions does the entropy of the system decrease ($\Delta S_{\text{sys}} < 0$)?
questions.solution:
Entropy of a system is largely dictated by the change in the number of gaseous moles ($\Delta n_g$):
- Option A: $\Delta n_g = 2 - (1 + 3) = -2$. The reaction consumes $4\text{ moles}$ of gas to produce $2\text{ moles}$ of gas, causing a substantial decrease in randomness ($\Delta S < 0$).
- Option B: $\Delta n_g = 1 - 0 = +1$ (gas is produced, $\Delta S > 0$).
- Option C: $\Delta n_g = 2 - 1 = +1$ (number of gas moles increases, $\Delta S > 0$).
- Option D: Solid to liquid phase transition increases molecular disorder ($\Delta S > 0$).

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] For an isolated system undergoing an irreversible spontaneous change, which of the following statements is ALWAYS true according to the Second Law of Thermodynamics?
questions.solution:
1. For an isolated system, no energy or matter is exchanged with the surroundings, so $q = 0$ and $w = 0$.
By the First Law of Thermodynamics: $\Delta U = q + w = 0$.
2. By the Second Law of Thermodynamics, the total entropy of an isolated system must strictly increase for any spontaneous (irreversible) process:
$$\Delta S_{\text{isolated}} = \Delta S_{\text{total}} > 0$$
Since the isolated system has no surroundings ($\Delta S_{\text{surr}} = 0$), we have $\Delta S_{\text{sys}} > 0$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] The boiling point of a liquid is $400\text{ K}$. If its enthalpy of vaporization is $\Delta H_{\text{vap}} = 40.0\text{ kJ/mol}$, the entropy of vaporization ($\Delta S_{\text{vap}}$) of the liquid at its boiling point is:
questions.solution:
At the normal boiling point, liquid and vapor exist in dynamic equilibrium at constant temperature and pressure, so $\Delta G_{\text{vap}} = 0$.
$$\Delta G_{\text{vap}} = \Delta H_{\text{vap}} - T_b \Delta S_{\text{vap}} = 0$$
$$\Delta S_{\text{vap}} = \frac{\Delta H_{\text{vap}}}{T_b}$$
Substitute $\Delta H_{\text{vap}} = 40.0\text{ kJ/mol} = 40000\text{ J/mol}$ and $T_b = 400\text{ K}$:
$$\Delta S_{\text{vap}} = \frac{40000\text{ J/mol}}{400\text{ K}} = 100\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] For a reaction to be spontaneous at all temperatures, the conditions on $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ must be:
questions.solution:
The Gibbs free energy change is given by:
$$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$
For a process to be spontaneous at all temperatures ($T > 0\text{ K}$), $\Delta G$ must be strictly negative irrespective of the numerical value of $T$:
- If $\Delta H < 0$ (negative) and $\Delta S > 0$ (positive), then $-T\Delta S$ is always negative.
- The sum of two negative numbers, $\Delta H + (-T\Delta S)$, is unconditionally negative ($\Delta G < 0$) at all positive temperatures.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] According to the Third Law of Thermodynamics, the absolute entropy of which of the following substances approaches zero as the temperature approaches absolute zero ($0\text{ K}$)?
questions.solution:
The Third Law of Thermodynamics (Nernst-Planck statement) states that the entropy of all perfectly crystalline pure substances approaches zero as the absolute temperature approaches absolute zero ($T \to 0\text{ K}$):
$$\lim_{T \to 0\text{ K}} S = 0$$
Substances with structural irregularities, random orientations, or amorphous solids (like $\text{CO}$, $\text{NO}$, $\text{N}_2\text{O}$, or glass) possess non-zero residual entropy even at $0\text{ K}$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] For the dimerization reaction $2\text{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)$, the standard enthalpy and entropy changes are $\Delta H^\circ = -57.2\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = -175.8\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$ respectively. The reaction is spontaneous:
questions.solution:
For spontaneity, $\Delta G^\circ < 0$:
$$\Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ < 0$$
$$-57200 - T(-175.8) < 0$$
$$-57200 + 175.8 T < 0$$
$$175.8 T < 57200 \implies T < \frac{57200}{175.8} \approx 325.37\text{ K} \approx 325.4\text{ K}$$
Thus, the dimerization is spontaneous only at temperatures below $325.4\text{ K}$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] The entropy of the universe during an irreversible spontaneous adiabatic process:
questions.solution:
For an adiabatic process, there is no heat exchange with the surroundings, so $q_{\text{surr}} = 0$, which gives:
$$\Delta S_{\text{surr}} = 0$$
For an irreversible spontaneous process within the system, internal friction and dissipation generate entropy:
$$\Delta S_{\text{sys}} > 0$$
Therefore, the total entropy change of the universe is:
$$\Delta S_{\text{univ}} = \Delta S_{\text{sys}} + \Delta S_{\text{surr}} > 0$$
Thus, the entropy of the universe always increases.

questions.question: At constant temperature and pressure, the decrease in Gibbs free energy ($-\Delta G$) represents:
options: Maximum non-expansion (useful) work done by the system
Total mechanical $P-V$ work done by the system
Total heat absorbed from the surroundings
Change in internal energy of the system
questions.solution:
By thermodynamic definition:
$$dG = dH - T dS - S dT = dU + P dV + V dP - T dS - S dT$$
From the First and Second Laws: $dU = dq_{\text{rev}} + dw_{\text{total}} = T dS + dw_{\text{total}}$.
At constant $T$ ($dT = 0$) and constant $P$ ($dP = 0$):
$$dG = T dS + dw_{\text{total}} + P dV - T dS = dw_{\text{total}} + P dV$$
Since total work is $w_{\text{total}} = w_{PV} + w_{\text{non-}PV} = -P dV + w_{\text{non-}PV}$:
$$dG = w_{\text{non-}PV} \implies -\Delta G = w_{\text{useful, max}}$$
Thus, $-\Delta G$ represents the maximum useful (non-expansion) work obtainable from the system.

questions.question:
[JEE Main 2023] Given the reaction:
$$\text{A}(s) \rightarrow \text{B}(s) + \text{C}(g)$$
If $\Delta H^\circ = +180\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = +150\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, the temperature at which the reaction attains equilibrium at $1\text{ bar}$ is:
questions.solution:
At equilibrium at standard pressure, $\Delta G^\circ = 0$:
$$\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T_{\text{eq}}\Delta S^\circ = 0$$
$$T_{\text{eq}} = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ}$$
Substitute $\Delta H^\circ = 180 \times 10^3\text{ J/mol}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = 150\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$:
$$T_{\text{eq}} = \frac{180000\text{ J/mol}}{150\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}} = 1200\text{ K}$$
Above $1200\text{ K}$, the reaction becomes spontaneous.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] An endothermic reaction has a positive entropy change. Which plot correctly describes the variation of $\Delta G$ with temperature $T$?
options: A straight line with negative slope and positive y-intercept
A straight line with positive slope and positive y-intercept
A straight line with negative slope and negative y-intercept
A straight line with positive slope and negative y-intercept
questions.solution:
From the Gibbs-Helmholtz relation:
$$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = -\Delta S \cdot T + \Delta H$$
Comparing with the linear equation $y = m x + c$ where $y = \Delta G$ and $x = T$:
- Slope $m = -\Delta S$
- Y-intercept $c = \Delta H$
Given:
1) Endothermic reaction $\implies \Delta H > 0$, so the y-intercept is positive.
2) Positive entropy change $\implies \Delta S > 0$, so the slope $m = -\Delta S$ is negative.
Therefore, the graph is a straight line with a negative slope and a positive y-intercept.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] When an egg is hard-boiled, the entropy of the system:
options: Increases due to denaturation of proteins
Decreases due to solidification of albumin
questions.solution:
During the boiling of an egg, heat causes the denaturation of globular proteins.
The compact, highly ordered helical secondary and tertiary structures of native albumin proteins unfold and unravel into random coil conformations.
This extensive unfolding and breaking of hydrogen bonds increases the disorder and molecular randomness of the polypeptide chains.
Consequently, the entropy of the system increases despite the visible macroscopic coagulation.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] For an ideal gas expanding isothermally into vacuum (free expansion), the values of $\Delta S_{\text{sys}}$, $\Delta S_{\text{surr}}$, and $\Delta S_{\text{total}}$ are:
questions.solution:
1. In free expansion, $w = 0$. Since it is isothermal, $\Delta T = 0 \implies \Delta U = 0$, which gives $q = 0$.
2. Since no heat is transferred to or from the surroundings, $q_{\text{surr}} = 0 \implies \Delta S_{\text{surr}} = 0$.
3. Since entropy is a state function, $\Delta S_{\text{sys}}$ is calculated along a reversible path connecting the same initial and final volume:
$$\Delta S_{\text{sys}} = nR \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right) > 0 \quad (\text{as } V_2 > V_1)$$
4. Total entropy change:
$$\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_{\text{sys}} + \Delta S_{\text{surr}} = \Delta S_{\text{sys}} + 0 > 0$$
(Confirming that free expansion is an irreversible, spontaneous process).

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] The standard entropies of $X_2$, $Y_2$, and $XY_3$ are $60$, $40$, and $50\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$ respectively. For the reaction $\frac{1}{2}X_2 + \frac{3}{2}Y_2 \rightleftharpoons XY_3$, to be at equilibrium, the value of $\Delta H$ at $300\text{ K}$ must be:
questions.solution:
Compute the standard entropy change of the reaction:
$$\Delta S^\circ = S^\circ(XY_3) - \left[\frac{1}{2}S^\circ(X_2) + \frac{3}{2}S^\circ(Y_2)\right]$$
$$\Delta S^\circ = 50 - \left[\frac{1}{2}(60) + \frac{3}{2}(40)\right] = 50 - [30 + 60] = 50 - 90 = -40\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$
For equilibrium at $T = 300\text{ K}$, $\Delta G^\circ = 0$:
$$\Delta H^\circ = T \Delta S^\circ = 300\text{ K} \times (-40\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}) = -12000\text{ J/mol} = -12.0\text{ kJ/mol}$$

questions.question: For a reversible process at equilibrium, which of the following is correct?
questions.solution:
For a system at true thermodynamic equilibrium:
1. Reversible processes represent state trajectories where the universe undergoes no net creation of entropy, so $\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_{\text{sys}} + \Delta S_{\text{surr}} = 0$.
2. Under conditions of constant temperature and pressure, the criterion for chemical equilibrium is $\Delta G = 0$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] The standard Gibbs energy change for the reaction $2\text{A} \rightleftharpoons \text{B} + \text{C}$ is $\Delta G^\circ = -11.5\text{ kJ/mol}$ at $298\text{ K}$. If the reaction quotient is $Q = 100$, in which direction will the reaction proceed spontaneously? (Take $RT \approx 2.478\text{ kJ/mol}$, $\ln 10 = 2.303$)
options: In the backward direction, because $\Delta G > 0$
In the forward direction, because $\Delta G < 0$
The reaction is at equilibrium, because $\Delta G = 0$
Cannot be determined without knowing $\Delta H$
questions.solution:
Calculate the actual Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G$ using:
$$\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT \ln Q$$
$$RT \ln Q = 2.478 \times 2.303 \times \log_{10}(100) = 2.478 \times 2.303 \times 2 = 11.41\text{ kJ/mol}$$
Now evaluate $\Delta G$:
$$\Delta G = -11.5\text{ kJ/mol} + 11.41\text{ kJ/mol} \approx -0.09\text{ kJ/mol}$$
Wait, if $\Delta G^\circ = -11.5$ and $RT \ln Q = 11.41$, then $\Delta G < 0$.
If $\Delta G^\circ = +5.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ or if $Q > K_{eq}$, the reaction proceeds in the backward direction.
Here $K_{eq} = e^{-\Delta G^\circ / RT} = e^{11.5 / 2.478} = e^{4.64} \approx 103.6$.
Since $Q = 100 < K_{eq} \approx 103.6$, $Q < K$, so the reaction proceeds forward, or with $Q = 200 > K_{eq}$, $Q > K$ so $\Delta G > 0$ and it shifts backward.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] The standard entropy change ($\Delta S^\circ$) for the reaction $2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ is negative. The reaction is spontaneous at $298\text{ K}$ because:
options: $\Delta H^\circ$ is highly negative such that $\Delta H^\circ < T\Delta S^\circ$
Liquid water has higher entropy than gases
questions.solution:
For the formation of liquid water from hydrogen and oxygen gases, the system loses gaseous moles, so $\Delta S_{\text{sys}}^\circ < 0$ (unfavorable entropy).
However, the formation of water is highly exothermic ($\Delta H^\circ = -571.6\text{ kJ}$).
Because of this large heat release into the surroundings, the entropy change of the surroundings is heavily positive:
$$\Delta S_{\text{surr}} = -\frac{\Delta H_{\text{sys}}}{T} > 0$$
This large positive $\Delta S_{\text{surr}}$ easily overcomes the negative $\Delta S_{\text{sys}}$, making $\Delta S_{\text{total}} > 0$, or equivalently $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S < 0$.

questions.question: [JEE Main 2023] Calculate the entropy change $\Delta S$ (in $\text{J/K}$) when $2\text{ moles}$ of an ideal monoatomic gas are heated from $300\text{ K}$ to $600\text{ K}$ at constant volume. (Take $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, $\ln 2 = 0.693$)
questions.solution:
At constant volume ($V_1 = V_2$):
$$\Delta S = n C_v \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)$$
For an ideal monoatomic gas, $C_v = \frac{3}{2}R$:
$$\Delta S = n\left(\frac{3}{2}R\right)\ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)$$
Substitute $n = 2\text{ mol}$, $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, and $\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{600}{300} = 2$:
$$\Delta S = 2 \times \frac{3}{2} \times 8.314 \times \ln(2) = 3 \times 8.314 \times 0.693$$
$$\Delta S = 24.942 \times 0.693 \approx 17.2848\text{ J/K} \approx 17.28\text{ J/K}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2022] For the vaporization of a liquid at $1\text{ atm}$, $\Delta H_{\text{vap}} = 30.0\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S_{\text{vap}} = 75.0\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$. Find the normal boiling point (in Kelvin) of the liquid.
questions.solution:
At the normal boiling point, liquid and vapor are in equilibrium at $1\text{ atm}$, so $\Delta G_{\text{vap}} = 0$:
$$T_b = \frac{\Delta H_{\text{vap}}}{\Delta S_{\text{vap}}}$$
Substitute $\Delta H_{\text{vap}} = 30.0 \times 10^3\text{ J/mol}$ and $\Delta S_{\text{vap}} = 75.0\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$:
$$T_b = \frac{30000}{75.0} = 400.0\text{ K}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2021] A reaction has $\Delta H = -110\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S = -150\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$. Find the value of $\Delta G$ (in $\text{kJ/mol}$) for this reaction at $300\text{ K}$.
questions.solution:
Using the Gibbs equation:
$$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$
Convert $\Delta S$ to $\text{kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$:
$$\Delta S = -150\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} = -0.150\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$
Substitute $T = 300\text{ K}$ and $\Delta H = -110\text{ kJ/mol}$:
$$\Delta G = -110 - [300 \times (-0.150)] = -110 - (-45) = -110 + 45 = -65.0\text{ kJ/mol}$$

questions.question:
[JEE Main 2023] Calculate the standard entropy of formation $\Delta S_f^\circ$ (in $\text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$) of $\text{CO}_2(g)$ at $298\text{ K}$ from the reaction:
$$\text{C}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g)$$
Given standard entropies: $S^\circ[\text{C}(s)] = 5.7\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, $S^\circ[\text{O}_2(g)] = 205.0\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, and $S^\circ[\text{CO}_2(g)] = 213.6\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The standard entropy of reaction is:
$$\Delta S_f^\circ = S^\circ[\text{CO}_2(g)] - \left(S^\circ[\text{C}(s)] + S^\circ[\text{O}_2(g)]\right)$$
Substitute the given values:
$$\Delta S_f^\circ = 213.6 - (5.7 + 205.0) = 213.6 - 210.7 = +2.9\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$

questions.question: [JEE Main 2020] For a reversible reaction, the equilibrium constant at $300\text{ K}$ is $K = 1$. Find the standard Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G^\circ$ (in Joules).
questions.solution:
The relationship between standard Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant is:
$$\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K$$
When $K = 1$:
$$\ln(1) = 0$$
$$\Delta G^\circ = -RT(0) = 0.0\text{ J}$$
